title: The truth shall make you free (John 8:31–32)
word: The truth shall make you free
hook: freedom comes from continuing in his word

segments.voice: Yesterday, the golden lampstands of Tabernacles and the light of the world. Your line was not in darkness.

Still in the temple, still the same long argument, and John points to some people in the crowd who have just come to believe in him. A teacher might greet new followers with a welcome. Jesus gives them a sentence that starts with a condition: if. The second half is famous on its own, and on its own it can sound like a slogan about facts. Today, the whole sentence, and how fast these new believers start arguing about who is free.
screen: `NEW BELIEVERS IN THE TEMPLE.` → `A SENTENCE THAT STARTS WITH IF.` → `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "If you continue in my word, you shall be my disciples indeed. And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." It begins with if. If you continue: stay, remain, keep living in my word. Freedom doesn't come at the start; it comes from staying. And truth here isn't first of all a fact you look up. In John's Gospel, truth is close to a person: later Jesus will say, I am the way, and the truth, and the life. Catholic readers hear knowing the truth as coming to know him, over time, by staying. His listeners bristle. We are Abraham's children, they say, and we've never been slaves to anyone. Jesus answers that he means another kind of slavery: "whosoever committeth sin, is the servant of sin." The thing you can't stop doing. The lie you have to keep up. The habit that runs you. Then: if the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed. Saint John Paul the Second's letter on moral life, The Splendor of Truth, keeps coming back to this verse. Freedom, he wrote, isn't doing whatever we like; it depends on truth and grows by living in it. Every lie needs guarding. Every truth you finally tell is one less thing to guard.
screen: `IF YOU CONTINUE IN MY WORD.` · `TRUTH: A PERSON, NOT ONLY A FACT.` · `THE SERVANT OF SIN.` · `FREEDOM DEPENDS ON TRUTH.` · then, large: `THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.`

segments.voice: Let one small thing come to mind that you haven't said: I'm the one who broke it, I'm actually not fine, I liked your idea more than I said. Notice how much effort it takes to keep it unsaid, and picture saying it, plainly and kindly. If you pray, ask for the courage to say it; if not, just hold it there a moment.
The truth shall make you free. Jesus's promise to those who continue in his word. In John, truth is close to a person. Today's word.
screen: `THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the truth sets free. Freedom grows by staying in his word. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear John 8:31–42 at a weekday Mass in the fifth week of Lent, and the Church's moral teaching, especially Saint John Paul II's Veritatis Splendor, draws on it to link freedom with truth.

chat.says: People quote "the truth shall make you free" all the time. What did Jesus actually mean?
options: It starts with if: if you continue in my word. Freedom from sin grows by staying with him.
That learning enough facts frees you, so the more you study, the freer you become.
That being Abraham's children already made his listeners free, with nothing more to do.
chat.meaning: The whole sentence begins, if you continue in my word. Jesus means freedom from being the servant of sin, which grows by staying.

notes: John 8 contains sharp exchanges; the script names the listeners as 'people who had come to believe in him' (8:31) and avoids collective labels. Confirm the framing (cf. Nostra Aetate 4).
'Carved over library doors and on university buildings' is general; no specific building named. Confirm.
Veritatis Splendor paraphrased (freedom depends on truth; VS 34, 84–87 cite John 8:32). Confirm.
Lectionary: John 8:31–42 on Wednesday of the Fifth Week of Lent. Confirm.
'Make your home in my word' as a gloss on menō: confirm.
